findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder appends the whole scratch buffer regardless of how many bytes were read
findings.impact: Any consumer that opts this decoder in receives a corrupted body: the value handed to the application contains stale bytes from earlier reads of the same archive, and a schema `pattern`, `maxLength` or `enum` check therefore runs against content the client did not send. Because the residue is bounded to bytes from the same request, no data crosses a user boundary; the effect is incorrect validation and corrupted payloads rather than disclosure.
findings.evidence: The read loop is `n, err := rc.Read(buffer); if 0 < n { content = append(content, buffer...) }`. It appends the full 256-byte scratch buffer rather than `buffer[:n]`, so every short read - the last read of every entry, and any partial read in between - contributes up to 255 bytes left over from the previous iteration. `buffer` is allocated once outside the entry loop and reused across all entries in the archive, so the residue also crosses from one zip entry into the tail of another. The decoded string is what the function returns to decodeBody, which hands it to schema validation and then to the application. The neighbouring documented hazard is separate and already acknowledged in the doc comment above the function ("may be susceptible to a zip bomb attack"): `io.Copy` into an in-memory buffer, then a full decompression with no cap.

findings.title: No permissions block in either workflow, so GITHUB_TOKEN inherits the repository default
findings.impact: Whatever the repository or organisation default for GITHUB_TOKEN is, every step of both workflows receives it - including the third-party code identified in F-003. If the default is read-write, a compromised upstream could push to the repository or alter releases; least privilege is not being expressed anywhere in the repository, so the answer depends entirely on a setting the code does not record.
findings.evidence: `grep -n permissions .github/workflows/*.yml` returns nothing: neither go.yml nor shellcheck.yml declares a `permissions:` block at workflow or job level. go.yml additionally binds the token into the job environment explicitly (`GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` under build-and-test env), which places it in the environment of every step in that job, including the unpinned third-party steps of F-003. Both workflows trigger on `push` as well as `pull_request`, so the default-branch runs are not covered by the reduced permissions GitHub applies to fork pull requests.

findings.title: A nil regex matcher is used after a failed pattern compile, panicking when MultiError is set
findings.impact: Every request carrying a string value for the affected schema panics inside validation. Under the shipped middleware net/http recovers per connection, so the client sees a dropped connection and the server logs a stack trace per attempt; where ValidateRequest is called outside net/http's recovery the process terminates. Unlike F-002 this needs no crafted payload - any well-formed request that reaches the schema triggers it, so it is a self-inflicted outage that an attacker can also drive deliberately once observed.
findings.evidence: openapi3/schema.go:2654-2666: on a cache miss the code calls `cp, err = schema.compilePattern(settings.regexCompiler)`; when that returns an error it returns early only if `!settings.multiError` (:2660-2662), otherwise it appends the error to `me` (:2663) and falls through to `if !cp.MatchString(value)` on :2666 with the failed `cp`. compilePattern (openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-32) assigns the compiler's result to the named return before testing err, so on the default path `cp, err = regexp.Compile(...)` leaves `cp` holding a typed-nil *regexp.Regexp - a non-nil interface whose MatchString dereferences a nil receiver - and on the custom-compiler path it leaves whatever nil the compiler returned. Either shape panics on :2666. The precondition is a pattern Go's RE2 engine cannot compile, which the library itself treats as an expected situation: openapi3/validation_options.go:80-84 ships D

findings.title: Three unchecked string assertions on document vendor extensions panic during Swagger 2 conversion
findings.impact: A document supplied by someone other than the operator crashes the conversion. The second principal is the author of the OpenAPI or Swagger file, and the boundary crossed is document into converting process - the case that matters for anything that converts specifications it did not write: a spec registry, a gateway that ingests uploads, a linting or diffing service, a CI job converting a vendor's file. The attacker gains a process abort of the conversion, not code execution or data access, which is why this is low.
findings.evidence: Four sites in one file read the same class of vendor extension out of a parsed document and cast it to string; one is guarded and three are not. Guarded, at :874-875: `value := schema.Value.Extensions["x-formData-name"]; originalName, _ := value.(string)`. Unguarded: :218-219 `if val, ok := schema.Value.Extensions["x-formData-name"]; ok { name = val.(string) }` in ToV3Parameter; :389-390 `if tempName, ok := schema.Value.Extensions["x-formData-name"]; ok { name = tempName.(string) }` in onlyOneReqBodyParam; :811-812 `if originalName, ok := requestBodyRef.Value.Extensions["x-originalParamName"]; ok { paramName = originalName.(string) }` in fromV3RequestBodies. The `ok` in each of those tests key presence, not type. findings.title: A non-standard HTTP method reaches PathItem.GetOperation, which panics by design, through the legacy router
findings.impact: One unauthenticated request aborts request processing before any validation runs - FindRoute is the first call the shipped middleware makes (openapi3filter/middleware.go:122). Under net/http the panic is recovered per connection, so the client's connection is dropped and the runtime writes a full goroutine stack trace to the server's error log; because the trigger costs the attacker a single short request and costs the server a stack dump plus a connection teardown, a loop is an amplified availability and log-volume attack rather than a plain flood. Where FindRoute or the exported GetOperation is called outside net/http's recovery - a worker, a CLI, a non-net/http transport, or consumer code doing `doc.Paths.Value(p).GetOperation(r.Method)` - the process terminates.
findings.evidence: openapi3/path_item.go:153-176 dispatches on the method string and its default arm is `panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))`. openapi2/path_item.go:112-131 is the same shape and additionally omits CONNECT and TRACE. The function carries no doc comment saying it panics. routers/legacy/router.go:108-153 feeds it the raw wire method: `method, url := req.Method, req.URL` at :109, then `node, paramValues := root.Match(method + " " + remainingPath)` at :141, and when that misses, `if route == nil { pathItem := doc.Paths.Value(remainingPath); if pathItem == nil { return ...ErrPathNotFound }; if pathItem.GetOperation(method) == nil {` at :146-150. findings.title: Unchecked type assertion in deepSet panics on colliding deepObject query keys
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client controls whether a panic occurs inside the request-validation path. Under the shipped middleware (openapi3filter/middleware.go:119-138, which calls ValidateRequest from an http.Handler) net/http recovers the panic per connection: the client's connection is dropped with no response and a full goroutine stack trace is written to the server's error log, so a cheap request loop yields connection churn and unbounded log growth. Where a consumer calls ValidateRequest outside net/http's recovery - its own goroutine, a worker pool, a CLI, or a non-net/http transport - the panic is unrecovered and terminates the process.
findings.evidence: deepSet (req_resp_decoder.go:899-908) walks a key path and creates intermediate maps: `if _, ok := m[key]; !ok { m[key] = make(map[string]any) }` followed by the unchecked `m = m[key].(map[string]any)` on line 905. The guard only creates a map when the key is ABSENT; when the key is present and holds a string, the assertion is executed against a string. makeObject (:911-933) feeds it from `for kk, value := range props` - a Go map, whose iteration order is randomized per range. A request carrying both, e.g. `?param[a]=x&param[a][b]=y`, therefore produces two entries whose deepSet order decides the outcome. findings.title: Options.SchemaValidationOptions and Options.RegexCompiler are silently not applied to parameter validation
findings.impact: An operator who installs document-scoped format validators - the use the field's own comment names - gets them enforced on request bodies and responses but not on query, path, header or cookie parameters, which is the surface reachable without a body at all. Values that the configured validator would reject pass parameter validation and are handed to the application as valid. The same asymmetry means a consumer cannot pass any per-validation option to parameter validation, including DisablePatternValidation, which is the documented escape hatch for the crash in F-007. The global pattern cache extends the unreliability to the body path: whether Options.RegexCompiler governs a given pattern depends on which request arrived first in that process.
findings.evidence: Three sibling call sites build a []openapi3.SchemaValidationOption from the same Options struct before calling VisitJSON, and they do not agree. ValidateParameter (validate_request.go:235-244) appends only MultiError, customSchemaErrorFunc and EnableJSONSchema2020 - it reads neither options.SchemaValidationOptions nor options.RegexCompiler, and `grep -rn SchemaValidationOptions` over the tree returns exactly two readers, both of wh

findings.title: Unbounded slice allocation from an attacker-controlled deepObject array index in query-parameter decoding
findings.impact: A single unauthenticated HTTP request with a short query string (a few dozen bytes) forces the validating process to allocate a slice sized by an integer the client chose, and then to iterate it. The result is memory exhaustion and process termination (Go runtime out-of-memory is not recoverable by the handler), or sustained CPU burn at lower indexes. Because openapi3filter is designed to run as request-validation middleware in front of the application (see openapi3filter/middleware.go), the crash takes the whole server down, not one handler. Repeated cheap requests give a reliable denial of service.
findings.evidence: Source: the raw query string. urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject, style "deepObject" (req_resp_decoder.go:660-681) extracts every bracketed segment of each query key with the regexp `\[(.*?)\]` and joins them into a nested props key. makeObject (:912-934) deepSets those into a nested map, then buildResObj (:970-995) hits the `array` branch and calls sliceMapToSlice(t). sliceMapToSlice (:938-960) does: `key, err := strconv.Atoi(k)` over the map keys, `max := -1; for _, k := range keys { if k > max { max = k } }`, then `for i := 0; i <= max; i++ { result = append(result, nil) }`. The only validation on the index is that it parses as an integer; nothing compares it against a configured maximum, the number of keys actually present, or any value the caller controls. buildResObj then does `resultArr := make([]any, len(arr))` and loops `for i := range arr` calling buildResObj once per slot, so the c

findings.title: CI executes third-party code from mutable references, including an unversioned go install
findings.impact: Anyone who gains control of one of these upstream references - a repointed tag, a compromised maintainer account, a hijacked module path - executes their code inside this repository's CI, with the workspace checked out and the runner's GITHUB_TOKEN in the environment. The goimports-reviser step is the widest: it is an individual-maintainer module, resolved at `@latest`, invoked with write access to every source file in the tree, so a malicious release could alter the source that the same run then tests and reports green.
findings.evidence: Nothing under .github/workflows is pinned by commit SHA. .github/workflows/go.yml uses actions/setup-go@v6, actions/cache@v3 and actions/checkout@v6; .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml uses actions/checkout@v2 and ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0. A git tag is a movable pointer, so none of these references is immutable. Beyond the actions, three steps fetch and execute Go modules resolved at run time: `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest` and `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest` in build-and-test, and - the sharpest of the three - `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` in check-goimports, which then runs over every .go file in the checked-out tree (`find . -type f -iname '*.go' ... -exec goimports-reviser {} \;`). `@latest` carries no version at all, so the build has no record of what it execut

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi has uncontrolled resource consumption in openapi3filter deepObject query parameter decoding
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

An uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client force multi-gigabyte heap allocation with a single, tiny HTTP request. When a spec declares a `deepObject`-style query parameter whose schema contains an array (a normal, documented pattern), the decoder reconstructs the array by reading the **largest attacker-supplied index** and allocating one slot for every position from `0` up to that index — *before* schema validation (including `maxItems`) ever runs. A request as small as 24 bytes (`?param[items][50000000]=x`) drives heap allocation to **~6.1 GiB**, reliably triggering an OOM kill / restart loop on memory-constrained services.

### Details

The OpenAPI `style: deepObject` serialization lets clients express arrays in the query string using bracket notation, e.g. `param[items][0]=a&param[items][1]=b`. The decoder first collects these into an intermediate `map[string]any` keyed by the string of the index, then converts that sparse map into a real `[]any` in [`sliceMapToSlice`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go#L936):
